idiom_name: interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); } with a Deque history
implementation_notes: The book's structure in Java: a two-method interface cannot be a lambda target, so commands stay small named classes or records holding the receiver and the parameters, and the invoker is an ArrayDeque used as a history stack. This remains the right shape when undo/redo is the requirement, because the JDK's own command contract - Runnable, a functional interface with a single run() - has no inverse and no history; the single-method case can still use a lambda or a method reference, which binds a receiver without declaring a class.
pitfalls: A two-method command is not a functional interface, so lambdas and method references cannot implement it; single-command lambdas must go through Runnable or a one-method interface.
ArrayDeque is not thread-safe: a shared invoker needs synchronization or a concurrent queue, and a command run on another thread must publish its captured state safely.
Lambdas capture effectively final variables only, and a captured this keeps the enclosing object alive for as long as the history holds the command.

variants.name: Runnable/Callable submitted to an ExecutorService
variants.implementation_notes: The queueing half of the pattern is standard library: Runnable is a functional interface whose single run() is the command contract, and Executor/ExecutorService is the invoker - its specification states it decouples task submission from the mechanics of how each task will run, executing the given command in a new thread, a pooled thread or the calling thread. Use it whenever the requirement is deferred, pooled, scheduled or asynchronous execution; it supplies no undo, no history and no replay, so logging or reversal must wrap the submitted task before it reaches the pool.
pitfalls: Runnable returns nothing and cannot throw checked exceptions; switch to Callable<T> and submit when the command produces a result or must report a checked failure.
Execution happens later on a pool thread, so captured receivers must be thread-safe and RejectedExecutionException must be handled when the pool or queue saturates.
The executor keeps no history: undo, audit and replay are lost unless a wrapper records the task (and its inverse) before handing it over.

variants.name: Sealed interface and records with exhaustive pattern switch
variants.idiom_name: sealed interface Edit with records + switch over record patterns
variants.implementation_notes: Since Java 21 the request set can be plain data: a sealed interface plus records per request, interpreted by a switch over record patterns. JEP 441 finalised pattern matching for switch and requires pattern switches to be exhaustive over sealed hierarchies, so the compiler proves that every request is handled, dispatch becomes a table jump instead of a virtual call, and the commands are immutable carriers that compare, serialise and hash for free. The trade is a closed set living in one module and behaviour living outside the command, which is why it complements rather than replaces the polymorphic form.
pitfalls: A sealed hierarchy is closed: a new request forces every switch over it to be revisited, which is the intended safety trade - keep the hierarchy in the module that owns the domain.
Behaviour moves out of the command into the switch, so operations needing private receiver state must expose it; guard against the switch growing into one god-method.
Exhaustiveness holds only while the switch is compiled against the same sealed interface and has no default branch; a default silently disables the completeness check.
